title: The ground of our asking (Revelations 41)
hookLine: Julian hears: I am the ground of your beseeching
tomorrow: a servant runs to obey and lands in a ditch. now what?

cards: Thirst shows up before any decision. Nobody plans to be thirsty; the body asks first, and then a hand reaches for the glass. A dry throat, a glance at the water bottle, and the hand is already moving.
So who starts a prayer? It seems obvious: the person praying. Someone wants something, asks for it, and waits to see whether God answers.
The asking comes first; God's part comes after. In chapter forty-one of her book, Julian of Norwich hears that order turned completely around.

teach.h: I AM GROUND OF THY BESEECHING.
teach.b: Our Lord, she says, showed her this: "I am Ground of thy beseeching." Beseeching is an old word for asking with your whole heart.

teach.h: HE WILLS IT, STIRS IT, THEN WE ASK.
teach.b: Then the order of events, as Julian heard it. First, it's God's will that you have the thing. Then God makes you want it.
Then God makes you ask for it, and you ask. So how could it be, she's told, that you wouldn't have what you ask for? The prayer you thought was yours started somewhere else.
Your asking is the last link in a chain that began with God wanting to give. Like thirst: the wanting arrives before the reaching. Julian draws a few things out of this.
Prayer isn't talking a reluctant God into something; the wanting was his first.
And when prayer feels like nothing, dry and barren, she hears that it's still very pleasing to God, even when we feel nothing and see nothing. So she's told to pray anyway.
Thanks belongs inside prayer too: an inward knowing, turning the whole self, with reverence and joy, toward what God is stirring.
Here's the one to tell a friend: Julian doesn't promise that every request turns out the way we pictured. What she gives is the root of it. The asking begins with him.

how: Readers of Julian of Norwich often take this chapter as encouragement to keep praying in dry seasons, and her line 'I am Ground of thy beseeching' is used in prayer and spiritual direction.

games.q: what does “the ground of our asking” mean?
o: the reason some prayers get answered more quickly
a list of the things Julian asked God for
Julian's teaching that God is the root of our prayer

games.q: the ground of our asking — tap the pairs.
p: God wills that you have it

s: for Julian, prayer works by persuading a reluctant God
the common picture. she hears the wanting was God's first; our asking is the last link.
Julian hears that dry, barren prayer is still pleasing to God
even when we feel nothing and see nothing.
Julian promises every request will turn out the way we pictured
she gives the root of prayer, not a guarantee about the shape of the answer.

games.q: your friend asks why anyone would pray if God already knows what's best. by Julian's chapter, what's the strongest reply?
o: prayer is how we talk God into helping.
God starts the wanting; asking joins in.
it makes no difference either way.
games.why: Julian hears: I am ground of thy beseeching. God wills it, stirs the wanting, then we ask. prayer joins what he's already doing.

practice: If there's water nearby, hold the glass a moment before you drink, and notice the thirst that came first. Take one slow sip and feel it land.

Without water, notice the breath instead: the body asks for air before you choose to breathe. For the rest of the sit, bring to mind one good thing you deeply want, and wonder whether that wanting, too, started on the other side.

wordCard.voice: The ground of our asking. Julian's teaching that God is the root of prayer: he wills it, stirs the wanting, and then we ask.

carryVoice: Carry this: he wants you to ask, because the asking was his idea first. Day sixteen-thirty-five, done.
